transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-01-17 15:00 UTC | Duration: 48m
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Ivy Chen (SE), Luis Romero (SRE) - Redwood; Maya Singh (CTO), Ethan Park (Platform Eng), Claire Ito (ML Eng), Rajiv Menon (Sec) - Orion Ventures

[00:00] Samir: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — p95/p99 tail latency, streaming vs non-streaming, kv cache behavior, batching, quantization tradeoffs, and networking in VPCs. we'll dig into what you're seeing and then propose a pilot.
[00:22] Maya: Thanks Samir. to set context, our user-facing chat has been fine at p50 but p99 spikes into the multiple seconds occasionally. we're seeing it on both streaming endpoints and non-streaming. curious about root causes.
[00:40] Ivy: ok, can you describe traffic pattern? token lengths, concurrency, are you using embeddings or multi-turn chat?
[00:50] Ethan: Mostly multi-turn chat, avg input tokens ~45, output ~90, concurrency 200-400 active users, bursts up to ~1k. we also do some background summarization non-streaming.
[01:10] Luis: quick hypothesis — tail often driven by cache misses (kv cache cold), large dynamic batches that overflow gpu mem, or network egress when requests route cross-region.
[01:30] Claire: we use a managed redis for kv cache in the same VPC. hit rates are approx 78% overall but drop significantly on new sessions. not sure if kv eviction policy is causing a lot of misses.
[01:50] Samir: that 78% helps but p99 is sensitive to the cold 22%. a few misses inline can cause kernel recompiles or longer kv fetch times, esp if redis node is noisy or a cross-az call happens.
[02:10] Ethan: when you say kernel recompile — do you mean on-device compilation or model warmup? sometimes inference nodes show a spike when quantized kernels swap in.
[02:22] Ivy: yes, two things — model warmup and JIT-like kernel selection. our runtime will pick optimized kernels based on sequence length/attention patterns; if an unusual seq length appears it can hit slower path. quantization can also change kernel selection and memory access patterns which affects latency.
[02:45] Maya: how big a factor is batching? we've seen recommendations to increase batch sizes to improve throughput but that seems to increase tail latency.
[02:58] Luis: batching is tradeoff. larger batches amortize GPU overhead so p50 improves, but p99 often increases because the slowest request in the batch delays all. dynamic batching helps but you need good batch timeouts and per-route SLOs.
[03:20] Samir: for our customers we often recommend small batch sizes with low timeouts for latency-critical routes and larger batch windows for background tasks. also prefix KV caching reduces per-token cost and latency for multi-turn chat.
[03:38] [04:00] Claire: curious about streaming vs non-streaming — streaming should reduce perceived latency, but we still see p99 spikes in streaming sessions.
[04:12] Ivy: streaming reduces time-to-first-byte but doesn't eliminate backend tail events. if the backend stalls (e.g., kv miss, disk pressure, or GC), streaming will expose jitter — you'll see a pause in the stream. so both need to be profiled.
[04:33] Ethan: network hops — we are in a single region but some services (auth, embeddings) are in a different region. Could that cause p99 spikes?
[04:45] Luis: absolutely. cross-region RPCs add ms to tens of ms depending. but transient DNS or routing issues can add hundreds in worst cases. also egress through NAT gateways in VPCs can add variability.
[05:05] Samir: quick example — a user request hits an LB, forwarded to inference node in us-west; inference node calls customer Redis in us-west-2, then calls an external embeddings service in us-east — that chain of hops multiplies tail risk.
[05:30] Maya: ok — what are mitigation levers? Dedicated? pinning model versions? caching layers?
[05:40] Ivy: common levers:
- move critical services into same AZ/region as inference (reduce cross-region hops)
- use Redwood Dedicated or reserved capacity to avoid noisy neighbor interference
- increase kv cache memory or switch to local in-process cache for hot prefixes
- tune batch timeouts / max batch sizes per route
- use quantization profiles that balance latency vs token quality (int8 vs int4)
[06:05] Ethan: we saw a 12% quality drop with aggressive int4 quant but 30% latency win — not acceptable for some flows.
[06:18] Ivy: yep that's the classic tradeoff. we recommend running A/B on small prompt evaluation sets. Redwood Optimize can suggest quant profiles by workload, but we still recommend manual evals.
[06:30] [08:00] Claire: about KV cache — you mentioned prefix caching and kv sharding. can you elaborate?
[08:12] Luis: sure. prefix cache stores repeated prefix tokens so you don't recompute attention for earlier tokens. for high-cardinality sessions shard caches across nodes so miss storms don't hit single redis. also use LRU with a slightly higher size for critical routes.
[08:35] Samir: additionally, local in-memory caches (per process) for the very hot prefixes cut network roundtrips; acceptable TTLs avoid staleness.
[08:50] Maya: what about cold-starts — initial requests after deploy cause p99 spikes?
[08:58] Ivy: cold-starts are common when models are paged out or kernels need to compile. mitigation: warmup runners before traffic, keep min replicas, or pin hot models on Dedicated. also pre-compile kernels for expected sequence lengths during deploy.
[09:20] Ethan: interesting. is there observability we can get? histograms, sampled traces?
[09:28] Luis: Redwood Console provides per-route p50/p95/p99 histograms, token-level latency breakdown (KV fetch, compute, network), and traces for sampled requests. we'll share a sample dashboard.
[09:40] Maya: can you explain how streaming vs non-streaming telemetry differ?
[09:48] Ivy: streaming traces include time-to-first-byte and chunk latency. non-streaming captures total time. both record internal stages. streaming often hides backend compute latency from end-user but you can still see chunk gaps where backend stalled.
[10:05] [12:00] Ethan: let's discuss a replication plan for our tests. we'd like to simulate production bursts with warm and cold cache states. suggestions?
[12:12] Ivy: recommended test matrix:
- Warm cache steady-state: run 10k requests over 10 minutes at target concurrency; capture percentiles.
- Cold cache spike: spin new session ids to force cold prefixes and run bursts to observe p99 delta.
- Streaming vs non-streaming: same prompt set, compare ttfb and overall completion time.
- Network fault injection: add artificial extra latency to redis and external services to measure sensitivity.
[12:45] Claire: any script templates?
[12:49] Ivy: yes, we'll share a locust/jmeter harness with streaming connector and headers to emulate session affinity.
[13:00] Samir: on the Dedicated side, recommended config for your concurrency (200-1k bursts) is x2 gpus per pod with a reservation that keeps a minimum of 3 runners warm; Luis will size it in the follow-up.
[13:17] Luis: for p99 stability I recommend reserving capacity and pinning to a model variant with predictable memory footprint; enable prefix caching local to runner and set batch max to 8 with a 10ms batch timeout for chat routes. background jobs can have batch max 64.
[13:38] Maya: what's the breakdown of latency we should expect in a good config?
[13:45] Ivy: example typical breakdown: TTFB ~40-60ms, compute 30-120ms depending on model & quant, kv fetch 5-30ms warm / 50-200ms cold, network overhead variable 5-100ms depending on hops. p99 usually dominated by cold kv, cross-region calls, or OOM/GC events.
[14:10] Ethan: You mentioned GC — have you seen JVM/Rust memory pressure cause latency spikes? we run some services on Java.
[14:20] Luis: yes, service-level GC pauses or swapping due to memory pressure can cause request queuing; ensure OS swappiness set low, provision enough mem, and prefer non-blocking containers for critical path. Redwood's inference processes are tuned to minimize GC but your side services can still impact.
[14:40] [16:00] Claire: about quantization — is there a recommended rollout path?
[16:08] Ivy: incremental: start with int8 for non-critical flows, run eval on small prompt sets, check hallucination/regression metrics. if acceptable, trial int4 on a subset and run A/B. Redwood Optimize will flag quality regressions.
[16:30] Maya: network-wise, is it feasible to colocate redis local to inference pods rather than a central redis?
[16:40] Luis: yes, local in-pod caches or sidecar caches are common. central redis is ok but for hot prefix workloads local caches reduce tail risk. tradeoff: consistency and memory overhead.
[17:00] Samir: a quick note on software fallbacks — we support automatic fallback to a smaller model variant when latency exceeds threshold; that limits p99 impact at cost of slight degrade in quality.
[17:15] Ethan: how do you detect and trigger that?
[17:20] Ivy: we use per-route latency SLOs and sliding-window detectors in our routing layer; when nodes breach thresholds, routing shifts to a faster variant or to Dedicated capacity.
[17:35] Maya: any tips for measuring the true network contribution?
[17:45] Luis: capture tcp-level RTTs at node, instrument service-to-service traces, and run synthetic pings between services during test windows. also measure NAT gateway metrics.
[18:00] [20:00] Claire: ok, let's go over a concrete pilot plan — what you'll send and what we'll run.
[20:10] Samir: we'll send: 1) locust harness + test matrix; 2) Redwood perf checklist; 3) sample console dashboard and traces; 4) SOC2 whitepaper. you run warm/cold runs and share histograms and sample traces. SE will propose Dedicated sizing and batch configs.
[20:34] Maya: timeline — we can run tests over next 3 days and regroup next week.
[20:40] Samir: perfect. any other questions?
[20:45] Rajiv: security quick Q — cross-region egress and encryption: how is traffic to our redis secured?
[20:53] Samir: we support VPC peering, private endpoints, and KMS-backed encryption for in-flight TLS + at-rest. we'll include our security docs.
[21:05] Ethan: for the benchmarking, do you recommend streaming tests with chunk sizes to simulate small tokens or larger chunks?
[21:12] Ivy: simulate both. small chunks increase overhead but reduce per-chunk compute; larger chunks reduce overhead but increase TTFB. we'll include recommended chunk sizes in the harness.
[21:30] [24:00] Maya: what are common surprises you've seen?
[24:08] Luis: surprises include: hidden 3rd-party calls in request paths, DNS timeouts, small disk I/O spikes (logs filling disk), and badly tuned batch timeouts that create microbursts.
[24:30] Claire: any quick heuristics for diagnosing live production p99?
[24:38] Ivy: capture a sample of p99 request IDs, run full breakdown (KV, compute, network). correlate timeline with infra metrics (CPU, nvlink, GPU mem, redis latency). often you'll see an outlier infra metric.
[24:58] Samir: ok let's recap.
[25:05] Samir: recap — send harness, perf checklist, security docs. Customer runs warm/cold tests and sends histograms and traces. Redwood proposes Dedicated sizing and batch/kv configs. Follow-up meeting next week to review results and pilot.
[25:30] Maya: thanks all.
[25:35] Ethan: thanks.
[25:40] Ivy: I'll share the repo and scripts after the call.
[25:45] Luis: will produce sizing and a sample config.
[25:50] Samir: meeting over.
